title: Measuring physical quantities
competency: Measure mass, length, time and temperature with the right instruments.

keywords.def: An instrument that measures mass by comparing it with a known mass.
A device that measures the temperature of an object or place.

en.text: Each quantity has its instruments. Balances measure mass, rulers, tapes and vernier calipers measure length, clocks and stopwatches measure time, and thermometers measure temperature. Use them carefully: zero the balance, start at the zero mark, hold a thermometer at the top.

am.text: ሚዛን መጠነ ቁስን፣ ማስመሪያና ቴፕ ርዝመትን፣ ሰዓት ጊዜን፣ ቴርሞሜትር ሙቀትን ይለካሉ። ሚዛኑ ዜሮ ማሳየቱን አረጋግጥ።

screens.title: At the clinic
screens.ask: A nurse wants to know if a child has a fever. Which instrument does she use?
screens.after: A thermometer measures temperature. A healthy body is about 37°C.

screens.title: Instruments in the lab
items: Measures mass. Check it reads zero first.
Measures temperature. Hold it at the top.
Measures the volume of a liquid.

screens.title: Mass and length
paras: Instruments that measure mass are balances. A balance compares a mass with a known mass.
Types: top pan, table, spring, platform and electronic balances.
Length is measured with a metre ruler, a measuring tape or a vernier caliper.
screens.note: Before weighing, put the balance on a level surface and check it reads zero.

screens.title: Time and temperature
paras: Time is measured with a stopwatch or a clock. Its SI unit is the second.
A thermometer measures temperature. The SI unit is the kelvin; °C and °F are also used.
Hold a thermometer at the top. Do not let the bulb touch the glass.
screens.note: Safety: never put a laboratory thermometer in your mouth.

screens.title: Zero error on a balance
screens.note: If the empty balance does not read zero, every reading is wrong by the same amount. Set it to zero before you weigh.

screens.title: Key words
defs: An instrument that measures mass by comparing it with a known mass.
A device that measures the temperature of an object or place.

screens.text: Measuring instruments: match each quantity with an instrument that measures it.
screens.why:
Mass: a balance, like an electronic balance.
Length: a ruler or tape; a vernier caliper for small lengths.
Time: a stopwatch or a clock.
Temperature: a thermometer.
screens.clue: What do you use to weigh? to time a race?

screens.text: Using a ruler: when you measure a pencil, where must one end of the pencil be?
opts: At the end of the ruler
screens.why:
A ruler counts from its zero mark.
Put one end of the pencil exactly on zero.
Read the scale at the other end.
That reading is the length.
If you start at the 1 cm mark, the reading is 1 cm too long.
screens.clue: Where does the ruler start counting?

screens.text: Thermometer safety, true or false: you may put a laboratory thermometer in your mouth if it is clean.
screens.why:
A laboratory thermometer is used with chemicals and hot liquids.
It is made of thin glass and can break.
The book says never put it in your mouth.
Cleaning does not make it safe. So it is false.

screens.text: Using a balance: what should it read before you put anything on it?
screens.why:
With nothing on it, the mass is zero.
So the balance must read zero.
If it reads 0.2 kg, every reading will be 0.2 kg too high.
Also check that it stands on a level surface.

screens.title: Which quantity?
screens.text: Measuring instruments: sort each instrument by the quantity it measures.
items: A thermometer measures how hot or cold.
It shows mass on a screen.
screens.why:
Balances (spring, electronic) measure mass.
A measuring tape and a vernier caliper measure length.
A stopwatch measures time.
A thermometer measures temperature.
screens.clue: Ask: what does this tool tell you, how heavy, how long, how much time, or how hot?

screens.text: Reading body temperature: two students measure 36.8°C and 38.5°C. What does this suggest?
opts: The second may have a fever
screens.ans: The second may have a fever
screens.why:
Normal body temperature is about 37°C.
36.8°C is very close to 37°C: normal.
38.5°C is 1.5°C above 37°C.
That is a sign of fever.
So the second student may have a fever.

screens.text: Zero error on a balance: Hirut's balance shows 0.2 kg with nothing on it. Her bag of sugar reads 2.2 kg. What is the real mass?
screens.why:
With nothing on it, the balance shows 0.2 kg.
So every reading is 0.2 kg too high.
Real mass = reading − 0.2 kg.
2.2 − 0.2 = 2.0 kg.
2.4 kg is wrong: you take away the extra, not add it.
screens.clue: What did the balance read with no load?

items.ask: Activity 1.4, body temperature: the standard body temperature is ___ °C
items.why:
A healthy human body stays near one temperature.
The book gives it as 37°C.
So the answer is 37.

items.text: Activity 1.5, using a thermometer: how should you hold it when measuring warm water?
opts: At the top, bulb not touching the glass
items.ans: At the top, bulb not touching the glass
items.why:
The bulb at the bottom senses the heat.
Hold the thermometer at the top, away from the bulb.
Keep the bulb in the water, not touching the glass.
If you hold the bulb, you measure your hand.
If it touches the glass, you measure the glass.

test.text: Instruments: what does a spring balance measure?
test.why:
A spring balance is a kind of balance.
Balances measure mass.
So a spring balance measures mass.
Time needs a clock; temperature a thermometer; length a ruler.

test.text: SI units: the SI unit of temperature is
test.why:
Temperature is a fundamental quantity.
Its SI unit is the kelvin (K).
Degree Celsius and degree Fahrenheit are also used, but they are not SI units.
So the answer is kelvin.

test.text: Instruments: which one measures small lengths very precisely?
test.why:
A vernier caliper has a fine extra scale.
It measures small lengths very precisely, like the width of a coin.
A stopwatch measures time; a thermometer, temperature.
A kubaya is a mug for volume.

test.text: Using a balance, true or false: it should be on a level surface before measuring.
test.why:
A balance on a slope gives wrong readings.
So first place it on a level, flat surface.
Then check that it reads zero.
So the statement is true.

test.text: Zero error on a balance: it reads 0.1 kg with nothing on it. A book reads 1.6 kg. What is the real mass?
test.why:
Empty, the balance shows 0.1 kg instead of 0.
So every reading is 0.1 kg too high.
1.6 − 0.1 = 1.5 kg.
So the book's real mass is 1.5 kg.

notes.text: p.14: "(0F)" is a misprint for °F (degree Fahrenheit).
